strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and important problem—safety alignment of Video LLMs—with a large-scale, real-world benchmark (VideoSafetyEval) spanning 19 subcategories, 6 principal risk categories, and 10 languages, substantially larger in scale than prior image-safety benchmarks (SIUO, SPA-VL, FigStep, VLGuard, MMBench, SafeBench).

Extensive empirical evaluation of 21 mainstream Video LLMs reveals a clear and interesting finding: integrating video modality substantially degrades safety performance (avg. 34.2% DSR drop) relative to text-only inputs, with controlled ablations (FPS, frame count, semantic harmfulness, video length) that help disentangle causes of this vulnerability.

Proposed defense framework VideoSafety-R1 (VST dataset + AT-SFT + Safety-guided GRPO) yields large, consistent safety gains across multiple video and image safety benchmarks (VSE-HH, MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) while only modestly affecting general video understanding capability, and outperforms several strong image-domain defense baselines (SPA-VL, MM-RLHF, Self-Reminder, VLGuard).

Very thorough appendix: dataset-quality verification via human annotation agreement (query/video label accuracy, analysis reliability), validation of the LLM-judge (Qwen-Long) against human labels and other frontier LLM judges, computational cost/latency analysis, cross-lingual analysis, attention-sink mechanistic analysis, and abundant qualitative case studies improve transparency and (partial) reproducibility.
Thoughtful ethics/reproducibility statement covering dataset access control, PII blurring, sensitive-word bias checking, and code release.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation pipeline (DSR, Helpfulness Score) relies on a single commercial LLM judge (Qwen-Long), and the training data (captions, harmfulness labels, CoT annotations) is generated largely by other Qwen-family models (Qwen-Max-VL, Qwen-Long). This creates a risk of circularity/family bias between the models used to construct training supervision and the model used to judge success, which is not fully addressed despite the reliability study in Appendix J.3.

Data construction (captioning, harmfulness classification, query generation, CoT generation) is almost entirely LLM-driven with only partial human spot-checks (1,000/10,000 samples), leaving open the possibility that systematic labeling biases or errors propagate through both the benchmark and the training/RL reward signals.

The false refusal rate (FRR) increases notably for VideoLLaMA3-2B+VideoSafety-R1 (+12.7%), which is a meaningful helpfulness/safety trade-off that is somewhat downplayed as 'acceptable' rather than critically analyzed.

Core technical contributions (alarm tokens as auxiliary classification heads, GRPO with rule-based dual-modality reward, dynamic reward adaptation) are largely recombinations of existing techniques (GRPO, attention-sink analysis, classifier-guided fine-tuning) rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, making the technical novelty moderate.

Case studies show fairly templated, repetitive refusal/justification language across different harm categories, consistent with the paper's own admission that CoT reasoning data (generated via fixed prompt templates and Qwen-Max) may lack naturalness/diversity — this raises concern about how much of the improvement reflects genuine safety reasoning versus template-matching optimized for the same-family judge.

Comparison baselines (SPA-VL, MM-RLHF, VLGuard, Self-Reminder) are only applied to Qwen2.5-VL-7B and trained with different data scales/recipes than VideoSafety-R1, making some head-to-head comparisons less controlled.

The claim that 'video modality degrades safety' is partly based on comparing full video input vs. text-only (no-vision) input, which are qualitatively different tasks (the model may simply default to refusal without visual context); the framing could be more nuanced regarding what portion of the drop is attributable to genuine unsafe multimodal reasoning versus lack of contextual grounding.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, real-world video safety benchmark (VideoSafetyEval) with 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 fine-grained risk subcategories and 10 languages, substantially larger in scale and category coverage than prior safety benchmarks (e.g., SafeBench, VLGuard, FigStep).

Provides a clear and fairly convincing empirical finding — that introducing video modality consistently and substantially degrades safety defenses relative to text-only inputs across 21 models (including commercial GPT-4o/Gemini) — which is a useful and underexplored observation for the community.

The proposed VideoSafety-R1 framework (alarm-token fine-tuning + safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation) shows large, consistent DSR improvements over the base model and outperforms several reasonable image-safety-defense baselines (Self-Reminder, SPA-VL, VLGuard, MM-RLHF) while also generalizing (with some help loss) to image safety benchmarks and general video understanding tasks.

Extensive appendix with ablations (component-wise ablation, hyperparameter sweeps, cross-lingual analysis, frame-rate/semantic-richness disentanglement, attention-sink visualization, computational cost, reasoning diversity, and qualitative case studies) demonstrates thorough empirical rigor and reasonable attempts at interpretability of the proposed mechanism.
Reasonable effort toward data-quality control and ethics: human verification of a sampled subset of labels/queries, sensitive-word bias checks, blurring of PII, and restricted dataset release plan.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metrics (DSR, Helpfulness Score) rely entirely on an automatic LLM judge (Qwen-Long); its reliability was validated on only 114 human-annotated samples, which is a fairly small sample given that all headline numbers throughout the paper (benchmarking 21 models, all ablations, cross-lingual results, etc.) depend on this judge.

There is a degree of methodological circularity: the same model family (Qwen-Max-VL/Qwen-Long) is used for video annotation, harmful/safe query generation, false-negative filtering, CoT data generation, AND final safety/helpfulness evaluation, which risks propagating systematic biases of that model family through the entire pipeline without independent cross-validation using a different judge model family at scale.

VideoSafety-R1 is only trained and demonstrated on relatively weak/small backbones (VideoLLaMA3-2B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B); the starting baseline (18.4% DSR for VideoLLaMA3-2B) is unusually low compared to other evaluated models (e.g., GPT-4o 73%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 86.7%, InternVL3-78B 74.4%), so the 'unprecedented' safety gains partly reflect starting from a weak baseline, and it remains unclear whether the method scales to stronger/larger backbones.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix Q) show some borderline behavior: in several cases the model's 'safe' response still elaborates on how the harmful risk/activity could be carried out or escalated (e.g., the risky-activities case) before refusing, suggesting the DSR metric may not fully capture partial-compliance leakage, and that the CoT refusals can be templated/formulaic rather than genuinely adaptive reasoning (acknowledged as a limitation by the authors themselves).

Technical novelty is incremental — alarm tokens are a straightforward extension of existing harmful-content classification heads to the video domain, and GRPO with rule-based classification rewards is a fairly direct combination of existing RL and chain-of-thought safety-training techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The dataset (the core benchmark contribution) is not released at submission time ("will be released publicly after further verification"), limiting immediate reproducibility of the primary resource, and no quantitative comparison is provided against concurrent, closely related video-safety benchmarks (VideoSafetyBench, SafeVid, Trust-VideoLLMs) beyond brief qualitative mentions.

strengths: Introduces VideoSafetyEval (VSE), by far the largest and most category-diverse video-LLM safety benchmark to date (11.4k video-query pairs, 19 subcategories, 10 languages), with a well-documented, multi-stage construction pipeline (static-video filtering via DINOv2, multi-agent harmful-element annotation, false-negative query checks).

Extensive and fairly rigorous data quality/reliability analysis: human verification of query/video/analysis labels (Appendix E), sensitivity-word bias checks, and reliability comparison of the LLM judge (Qwen-Long) against several commercial models with accuracy/F1/cost tradeoffs (Appendix J.3) — this substantially strengthens confidence in the benchmark and evaluation metric.

The core empirical finding — that adding the video modality substantially degrades safety relative to text-only mode across 21 models (up to 34.2% average DSR drop, even for GPT-4o and Gemini) — is a novel, well-supported, and practically important observation for the field.

VideoSafety-R1 shows large and consistent safety gains across in-domain (VSE-HH) and out-of-domain settings (image benchmarks MMBench/VLGuard/FigStep, cross-lingual settings, visual-attack variant VSE-HH-VA, and varying video length/FPS), while general video-understanding capability degradation is modest (~0.66% average drop across MVBench/VideoMME/PerceptionTest/NextQA/VideoHallucer).

Thorough ablation studies (Table 6/18) cleanly isolate contributions of AT-SFT alarm tokens, classification tasks, GRPO, and DRA, and the attention-sink analysis (Fig. 7) provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for why alarm-token fine-tuning improves safety perception.

Comprehensive appendices (59 pages) covering dataset statistics, taxonomy comparison to prior safety benchmarks, hyperparameter sensitivity, computational cost analysis, and 19 illustrative qualitative cases, substantially aiding reproducibility and interpretability.
weaknesses: The core evaluation metric (DSR/S_Help) relies entirely on an LLM judge (Qwen-Long); although reliability is checked against 114 human-labeled samples, this is a fairly small validation set given the scale of the benchmark and the many fine-grained conclusions drawn (e.g., 19-subcategory breakdowns, cross-lingual analysis) — errors or judge biases could propagate into many reported numbers without deeper stratified verification.

VideoSafety-R1 is trained and most heavily evaluated starting from VideoLLaMA3-2B, a relatively weak/older backbone; the Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B extension is somewhat less thoroughly ablated, and it's unclear how well the framework would scale to stronger/larger video LLMs (e.g., 32B/72B) or whether gains would diminish given the paper's own observation that these already have relatively high baseline DSR.

The safety training data (VST) and thinking-chain annotations are template-generated using Qwen-Max prompts with fixed refusal boiler-plate patterns (as shown in Appendix Q cases and R.8 examples), raising concerns about response diversity/naturalness and potential overfitting to a narrow refusal style — the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this but does not quantify how it affects generalization to more naturalistic jailbreaks or novel attack forms beyond the benchmark's own construction pipeline.

The FRR increase on VideoLLaMA3-2B (+12.7%) after VideoSafety-R1 training indicates a non-trivial over-defensiveness/false-refusal side effect for one of the two backbones, and the qualitative case in Fig. 25/26 (Misinformation/Generated Information) shows some over-cautious behavior even on plausibly benign content, suggesting the safety-helpfulness tradeoff is not fully solved.

Some methodological choices (weighting coefficients, dynamic reward adaptation ranges, use of ROUGE similarity as part of reward) are heuristic and set largely by limited grid search (Table 15) without deeper theoretical justification, and reliance on a single commercial LLM (Qwen-Max/Qwen-Long) for nearly the entire pipeline (annotation, query generation, evaluation) creates a potential single point of systematic bias that is only partially probed.
